title: Claude-generated apps can now be installed on the desktop: Artifacts launches 'Install as app', turning tools created from a single sentence into standalone software

content_html:
Small apps whipped up live with Claude used to be able to live only in browser tabs—close the tab, and they disappeared with it. On November 25, Anthropic launched an “Install as app” option for interactive Artifacts, letting users install generated apps as standalone software directly onto macOS and Windows desktops. The tool that AI generates from a one-sentence description now has its own desktop icon.

Once installed, an Artifacts app feels similar to installing a web app on your computer: it has its own desktop toolbar icon, so you no longer have to go through browser tabs to access it; click the icon and it launches directly. Generated content and system-level software are now separated by only the thinnest of barriers.

For permissions, Anthropic offers three tiers. The most conservative is the default permission mode, in which the app runs much like a browser tab and stays in its lane; one step further, users can grant additional app permissions—allowing it to send notifications, intercept keyboard shortcuts, and appear above other app windows; those feeling bold enough can even grant an installed Artifacts app full computer access. Different permission configurations directly determine which system features and operations the app can use and perform, and the choice always remains in the user’s hands.

The feature is currently in beta and is gradually rolling out to macOS and Windows desktop users. The significance of this update is that Artifacts is no longer just an interactive canvas in the browser, but is beginning to evolve toward a true lightweight app distribution model—when “say one sentence to AI and get software you can install on your computer” becomes routine, the barrier to app development and distribution has been pried down another notch.
